content: The Monitoring and Improvement subgroup of the HIVResNet Working Group on the Prevention of HIV Drug Resistance and Quality of Care has emphasized the importance of incorporating patient experience indicators into national quality improvement frameworks. This aligns with the 2018 Lancet Global Health Commission report on High-Quality Health Systems in the Sustainable Development Goals era, which identified positive user experience as a critical component of high-quality health services. The report proposed illustrative indicators, such as patient-reported experience measures, to assess the avoidance of healthcare services due to stigma and discrimination, particularly among key populations. The WHO standards for maternal and newborn care include communication and dignity-focused standards (Standards 4 and 5), which can be adapted for HIV programs. However, further efforts are needed to capture dimensions of service quality, such as compassion and patient experience. WHO is actively working on standardizing methodological approaches to address these aspects. Additionally, indicators reflecting community engagement and demand-side factors, such as satisfaction with clinical services and community perceptions of high-quality healthcare, are essential. These perceptions may vary across different cultural and geographical settings. HIV programs in many countries already have established quality management processes, offering opportunities for integration with national quality policies and strategies. These programs can serve as pathfinders for broader national quality initiatives, providing valuable lessons and a foundation for scaling up quality management efforts. They also present entry points for strengthening national systems for quality care. Community-led monitoring is a vital tool for improving healthcare quality. It enables individuals living with and affected by HIV to assess the quality, effectiveness, and accessibility of health programs and services. This approach places care recipients at the center of monitoring and advocacy efforts, utilizing various community-led methodologies in collaboration with key stakeholders. Community-led monitoring can be conducted by independent local organizations or committees of community representatives at local, national, regional, and global levels. Its foundation lies in comprehensive HIV prevention and treatment education, empowering communities to identify relevant indicators for tracking over time. Communities collect both quantitative and qualitative data to evaluate the acceptability, availability, and accessibility of services. This process should be routine and conducted at least semiannually in collaboration with local healthcare officials. The goal is to enable care recipients to provide structured, evidence-based input on healthcare services through a collaborative and solutions-oriented process. Metrics for assessment and feedback must be tailored to the healthcare needs identified by local communities. Through a consultative process, communities support the development of metrics, measures, and tools for community-led monitoring and advocacy. Community-led monitoring involves five key steps: data collection, analysis and translation, engagement and dissemination, advocacy, and monitoring changes. Examples of community-led monitoring models include suggestion boxes, client satisfaction surveys, health facility committees, and comprehensive community treatment observatories. Feedback mechanisms should ideally be present at each service point or health unit rather than being centralized in larger facilities. Healthcare staff should routinely review feedback, and visible action to address concerns must be prioritized. Routine, structured community-led monitoring and active patient feedback mechanisms empower patients to take ownership of their healthcare services and provide a voice in shaping service standards, availability, and accessibility. This process fosters accountability among service providers and local and national officials, leading to improved health outcomes. Multilateral donors and normative agencies, such as PEPFAR, the Global Fund, and UNAIDS, have increasingly recognized the importance of community-led monitoring and advocacy, requiring recipient countries to include these efforts in costed work plans. HIV programs must implement and sustain quality management systems to achieve the 95–95–95 targets, reduce morbidity and mortality, and meet Sustainable Development Goals. Existing quality improvement efforts have demonstrated positive impacts on clinical outcomes but require sustained resource commitment from health ministries. Evidence on the sustainability and cost-effectiveness of quality assurance and improvement efforts remains limited, necessitating strengthened efforts to foster a culture of quality awareness. Addressing these challenges requires planning, collaboration with health ministries and stakeholders, community involvement, and partnerships with local organizations and donor agencies. Organizational cultures, local systems, and infrastructure, including information systems for routine program data collection, must also be adapted to support high-quality health services. The current momentum toward high-quality health systems presents an opportunity to scale up quality management efforts within HIV programs, particularly in the context of universal health coverage and the United Nations High-Level Meeting on Universal Health Coverage. Procurement and supply management systems for HIV health products must ensure the continuous availability of effective, quality-assured antiretroviral (ARV) drugs, diagnostics, and consumables at service delivery sites. This requires integrated national strategies that consider available resources and enable robust procurement and supply management systems. All individuals living with HIV should have access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, necessitating accelerated ART program scale-up. Challenges in implementing WHO recommendations for ARV drugs and diagnostics include product selection, demand forecasting, procurement planning, storage and distribution, monitoring consumption, and addressing risks of stock-outs or expired products. These issues can be mitigated through national stakeholder working groups involving policymakers, implementers, funders, and supply chain specialists. Medicines and diagnostic products should align with national guidelines and program needs. WHO recommends minimizing the number of ARV regimens to optimize treatment and sourcing. Countries must ensure that selected products are registered and included in national essential medicines lists. Transition plans should be developed to phase out outdated products and introduce new guidelines in a synchronized manner to minimize waste and shortages. Quantifying and forecasting demand for ARV drugs and diagnostics requires detailed knowledge of treatment numbers, regimens, scale-up rates, and product registration status. For diagnostics, quantification should account for the number of individuals requiring testing and the specific test types needed.
